discriminating_test: Extract unWISE time-resolved W1/W2 coadds for this source and for nearby comparison stars of the same W1 brightness. If the source alone shows a ~0.4 mag W1 rise in 2015, with W2 rising more, the warm dust is real. If the comparison stars show the same trend, it is a NEOWISE faint-source bias, which leaves Gaia calibration as the leading explanation.

evidence.feature: Coherent monotonic fade in G, BP and RP (slope_z -10.9, abbe 0.14, depth_g 0.030), plateau near 0.989 for the last ~175 d
NEOWISE W1 0.60-0.77 at t=-219 to 331, then 0.94-0.96 at t=504-864 and ~1.07 later: ~+45% step coinciding with the G drop, matching W1_pred_dust_shell_1000K = 0.47
Pipeline W1 inside-vs-outside change -0.075+/-0.125, consistent with no IR change confined to the dip window
G drops occur across data gaps (302-357 d and 733-829 d), step-like, possibly at calibration-epoch boundaries
sigma_visit 0.0043 equals the errors; dense transit groups at 458 d and 1004 d show no modulation above ~0.5%
ruwe 0.979, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal bp_rp excess factor 1.19
AllWISE W1-W2 = 0.1 and Ks-W1 = 0.2 (no strong excess in 2010); ZTF g/r/i flat to <1% over ~7 yr
BP/RP depth ratio 1.69+/-1.38 (z_grey 0.5, z_dust 0.0): uninformative on grain size
Single-epoch RP outliers at t=457.8 and 679.1 d (0.84) absent in G

explanation: Most probable: warm circumstellar dust appearing around an otherwise quiet G-type star. G, BP and RP come from independent instruments, and all three fade together by about 3-4% over about 500 d, in steps that fall in data gaps, then level off. The BP/RP ratio of 1.69+/-1.38 does not separate dust from grey blocking. NEOWISE W1 sits at 0.60-0.77 before t~350 and at about 0.95-1.07 afterwards. That rise of about 45% matches the 0.47 predicted for 1000 K re-emission. The pipeline's in-versus-out W1 test misses it because the brightening persists after the change. There is no rotational scatter and nothing points to a blend. Still possible: Gaia calibration steps plus a NEOWISE trend that is only a faint-source bias, a disk occultation, or an activity cycle.

discriminating_test: Get archival multi-epoch photometry from 2003-2013 (SDSS, Pan-STARRS, Catalina) to find when the fade began and the shape of its ingress. A disk ingress shows a start and curvature (S-shaped coverage). An injected ramp runs straight back. Follow up with one spectrum to look for shell absorption lines.

evidence.feature: BP/RP depth ratio 0.999 +/- 0.156 (z_dust -4.5), G depth equal to BP and RP
W1 and W2 decline about 22-27% over 10 yr, the same fractional rate as optical
Same linear trend in Gaia, ZTF PSF (2 arcsec) and WISE (6 arcsec) photometry; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.01
Independent surveys share one constant absolute slope; Gaia drift already removed
Abbe 0.027, no non-recurring dips, no curvature across 12 yr; perfectly linear ramp
Ks(2000) - W1(2010) = 0.1 and G-Ks 2.3 are photospheric, so the fade began after about 2000-2010
No warm IR excess (W1-W3 about 0), so the absorber is localized or cold
Significant parallax, stellar W1-W2, colour of a K giant

explanation: A quiet K giant (M_G about 1, R about 10 Rsun, halo distance) fades smoothly and linearly in flux at about 2.2-2.6%/yr from 2013 to 2025, by about 25%, at the same fractional rate in Gaia G/BP/RP (ratio 0.999), ZTF g/r/i and NEOWISE W1/W2. Independent instruments with very different apertures rule out blends and calibration drift. Matching W1/W2 dimming rules out a cooling star and small-grain dust. The best natural fit is the long ingress of a large-grain or optically thick disk around a wide companion, which needs a soft edge or a very slow crossing. The perfectly linear, grey ramp with no curvature also looks like an injection, which keeps unexplained high.

discriminating_test: Inspect the Gaia per-CCD G and BP/RP epoch data and scan angles for the t~829-840 transits. A neighbour in the window or edge flux loss at those scan angles would make the decline instrumental, while a coherent chromatic dip in BP/RP would favour the star.

evidence.feature: slope_z -1.02, abbe 1.22, n_below_3sigma 0: the change is not statistically significant
Lowest G fluxes at t 829.6, 829.7 and 840.2 carry 2-5x the median error, and fov1/fov2 disagree at 840.1 vs 840.2
FoV-pair disagreements at 679 (1.009 vs 1.001) and 829 (1.011 vs 0.983)
G-Ks ~3.4: a cool, probably M dwarf, where ~1% slow spot or activity changes are common
NEOWISE W1 change 0.0001 +/- 0.007 against a 1000 K shell prediction of +0.20; W2 below the 300 K shell prediction
ZTF g/r/i flat after 2020 and no recurrent dips in 2000+ epochs
BP/RP depths and colour ratio null, so achromatic versus reddened cannot be tested

explanation: The detected 'drop' is a marginal ~1% decline over 11 Gaia visits. sigma_visit is 1.1%, slope_z is -1.0, abbe is 1.22 (noise-like) and no epoch lies beyond 3 sigma. The lowest points (t~829.6-840.2) are the transits with inflated errors (0.007-0.015), and fov 1 and fov 2 disagree within those pairs, which points to a few poorly measured transits rather than a coherent change on the star. G-Ks~3.4 suggests a cool, probably M-type dwarf, so slow spot evolution at the 1% level is the leading astrophysical option. No BP/RP colour is available. ZTF shows no level change, and NEOWISE W1/W2 are flat. This rules out warm dust shells and is consistent with anything small.

discriminating_test: Use ATLAS forced photometry (or ASAS-SN or Pan-STARRS) from 2015-2017, which overlaps the Gaia epochs, to check whether the same two steps appear at the same dates. Compare absolute calibrated magnitudes before and after Gaia to see whether the star recovered.

evidence.feature: Three flat plateaus (1.027, 1.002, 0.972 in G) consistent in fov 1 and 2 and across many scan groups
G, BP and RP all fade together by similar fractions; no single-epoch or single-band behaviour
Changes are abrupt steps with no in-plateau trend, falling exactly in observing gaps
Steps align with time intervals rather than scan geometry; could mimic calibration-epoch offsets
BP/RP depth ratio 1.23 +- 0.59, consistent with grey, dust or cooling
No IR excess (Ks-W1 0.1, W1-W2 0.0), high-latitude G dwarf (M_G ~4.8)
NEOWISE W1 change -0.01 +- 0.058 vs +0.41 predicted for a 1000 K shell
ZTF 2018-2025 flat in g, r and i with low scatter
ruwe 0.993, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor

explanation: G, BP and RP drop in two discrete steps (about 2.5% near t~400, then 3% near t~780), each inside a ~100-day scanning gap, with plateaus flat to ~0.3% across both fields of view and many scan groups. So the change is time-ordered, not scan-angle blending, and seen in all bands. The fade is mildly bluer (BP/RP 1.2+-0.6), the star is a quiet G dwarf at 2 kpc with no IR excess, and NEOWISE excludes only a hot shell. The best natural fit is staged ingress of a structured circumstellar or circumsecondary occulter. But the step-and-flat-plateau shape fits no common process well, so an artificial signal or a per-source Gaia calibration offset remains likely. ZTF is self-normalised and cannot show recovery.

discriminating_test: Check independent photometry that overlaps Gaia days ~400-1000 (ATLAS forced photometry or Catalina/Pan-STARRS seasonal means). If the ~2.5% drop appears at the same dates, the change is real, and Gaia DR4 epochs would then show whether an egress follows. If not, the step is instrumental.

evidence.feature: G flat at ~1.022 for days 0-554, then ~1.000 at day 679 declining to ~0.988 by day 1004 (abbe 0.154, slope_z -7.6)
Step seen equally in fov 1 and fov 2
BP depth 0.044+-0.025, RP depth 0.038+-0.016, G 0.027; ratio 1.13+-0.81 consistent with grey
Duration >=325 d with depth 2.7%: t ~ 2R/v needs v << 1 km/s for a stellar occulter
ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp_excess 1.2 normal; step monotonic in time rather than recurring with scan geometry
W1-W2 ~ -0.2, Ks-W1 ~ -0.3: stellar colours, no warm excess, NEOWISE W1 change -0.012+-0.079
High galactic latitude, bp_rp 0.77, parallax_snr 2.7: likely old distant G dwarf, no IR excess
ZTF 2018-2024 flat season to season (<0.5%), so no ongoing 3% activity cycle, but per-field normalisation hides absolute level
Single abrupt step in a G=17.5 star in Gaia-only epochs; star-specific calibration or cross-match step cannot be excluded from packet

explanation: In G the star sits flat at about 1.022 until day 554, drops about 2.2% before day 679 and keeps fading slowly (about 1% more) to the last visit. Both fields of view show it, and BP (about 4%) and RP (about 3%) agree with a grey change. That points to a real change in flux rather than a G-only or FoV offset. The most likely single cause is the start of a long, shallow, grey occultation by a disk or dust structure. A 325+ day stellar eclipse would need an impossibly slow orbit. The quiet, dwarf-like colours and the absence of any infrared excess or NEOWISE change fit. ZTF is flat but normalised per field, so it cannot show whether the star recovered. A star-specific Gaia calibration or cross-match step is still quite possible.

discriminating_test: Retrieve absolutely calibrated (un-normalised) photometry from 2017-2019, e.g. Pan-STARRS, ASAS-SN or ZTF zero-pointed magnitudes, plus NEOWISE W1/W2 trends, to see whether the star stayed at the faded level or recovered, and whether the fade is reddened or comes with an infrared excess.

evidence.feature: Smooth multi-year G decline (abbe 0.1, slope -1.79%/yr, slope_z -8.4) steepening to a 3.8% plateau at the end
fov 1 and fov 2 transits agree within errors during the fade (e.g. 913.9/914.1, 929.86/929.94)
ruwe 1.05, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.18 (normal for bp_rp 0.76)
BP/RP depth ratio 1.33+/-0.42 (z_grey 0.79, z_dust -0.88): fade is in all bands, colour ambiguous
Fade lasts at least 88 d with gradual ingress; t ~ 2R/v implies v < 1 km/s for a stellar-size occulter
F/G dwarf or subgiant (M_G ~4) at 2.6 kpc and |b| 20-25 deg, i.e. ~1 kpc off the plane, likely old
Parallax SNR 7.4 and stellar colour
Old quiet star: a ~5% activity-cycle amplitude is implausible
ZTF g/r flat after 2018 (no change after 2020, no slope), but normalised per field so the level relative to Gaia is unknown
No WISE/NEOWISE data in or around the fade, so no energy-budget or IR-excess test

explanation: Most probable: a slow, mildly reddened occultation by extended circumstellar or circumsecondary dust. Gaia G declines smoothly (abbe 0.1, slope_z -8.4) by about 5% over 1000 d, steepening to a 3.8% deficit in the last 90 d. The decline shows in both fields of view and in BP and RP alike (BP/RP ratio 1.33+/-0.42, consistent with grey or dust). Low ruwe, zero multi-peak fraction and a normal BP/RP excess argue against a neighbour, and the shared calibration drift has been removed. For an old F/G dwarf about 1 kpc off the plane, activity cycles this large are unlikely, and a stellar eclipse lasting this long needs orbital speeds well below 1 km/s. With no IR data and ZTF normalised per field, the cause is only weakly constrained.

discriminating_test: Run forced photometry on unWISE/NEOWISE time-resolved coadds in W1 and W2. This confirms or refutes the ~0.6 mag W1 brightening after t~600 at proper S/N and measures W1-W2 for the dust temperature. Also compare Pan-STARRS (pre-2015) with ZTF/Gaia absolute magnitudes to check that the optical deficit persists.

evidence.feature: NEOWISE W1 brightens ~80% (0.58 to ~1.05 of median) between t=504 and t=865, at the same time as the G fade, and stays high afterwards
W1 rise matches W1_pred_dust_shell_1000K = +0.70 for the 7% G depth; the 300 K and grey predictions do not match
Smooth monotonic fade (abbe 0.079, slope_z -9.52) seen in both fov 1 and fov 2 across many transit groups
ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor: no resolved neighbour
W1-W2 ~0.2 and normal excess factor: point source without AGN-like IR colours
parallax_snr 2.8 at G=18.6 with bp_rp 1.22 fits a distant K dwarf rather than a supergiant
W1=16.5 is near the NEOWISE single-exposure limit, so the visit means may be biased and the quoted errors may be too small
BP/RP depths 0.037+-0.085 and 0.065+-0.042: colour of the fade cannot be determined
Fade confined to a single slow 7% episode at G=18.6 after calibration-drift removal

explanation: Most likely circumstellar dust, such as hot debris from a collision, around a faint K-type star that is probably a dwarf. G fades smoothly by about 7% from t~500 to t~880 and stays faint to the last visit. Both fields of view agree (abbe 0.08, slope_z -9.5), so it is not a single-epoch or FOV artefact. NEOWISE W1 rises at the same time, from ~0.58 to ~1.0-1.1 of its median between t=504 and t=865, and stays high to t=3414. That is close to the +0.70 the pipeline predicts for a 1000 K shell absorbing 7% of the starlight. BP and RP are too noisy to test the colour. The main doubts are W1 reliability near the NEOWISE single-exposure limit and a slow Gaia processing drift at G=18.6.

discriminating_test: Check Gaia DR3 epoch photometry of field stars with similar G and colour on the same scans for a step between t~555 and t~679. Also compare absolute-calibrated pre-2016 survey photometry (e.g. Pan-STARRS) with later ZTF/Pan-STARRS mean magnitudes to see whether a ~4% drop is real and lasting.

evidence.feature: Fade is a sharp step across a 124-d gap, then flat at ~0.967 for 323 d, ending faint at the last visit
Step is present in both fov 1 and fov 2
sigma_visit 0.0053 below the median error 0.0072: no spot modulation or short-term variability
BP and RP depths (0.006+-0.055, 0.023+-0.032) consistent with the G depth but give no colour constraint (z_grey -0.3, z_dust -0.6)
NEOWISE W2 change -0.03+-0.23 against +0.94 predicted for a 1000 K shell; W1 too noisy to tell grey blocking from a cooling star
Photospheric G-Ks, Ks-W1, W1-W2 colours; no IR excess
ruwe 1.04, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor: no sign of a neighbour or companion
Parallax SNR 3 at G=18 with bp_rp 1.22 implies a K dwarf, not a distant giant
ZTF 2018+ flat and change after 2020 ~0, but normalised per field, so the Gaia step cannot be checked

explanation: The dip is a clean ~4.3% step in Gaia G that falls inside a 124-day visit gap (t 555-679). The star then stays flat at ~0.967 until the last visit, in both fields of view. Before the step the star is quiet (sigma_visit 0.5%). ZTF covers only later years and is normalised per field, so it cannot confirm the step's level. BP/RP errors are too large to give a colour, and WISE is too noisy to test for grey dimming or a temperature change; it does rule out a hot dust shell. The star is a faint K dwarf with no IR excess and no sign of a companion or neighbour. My leading explanation is a step in Gaia's calibration or processing that affects this source alone. A slow change in the star, or a long occultation, remains possible.

discriminating_test: Take a moderate-resolution spectrum now and compare it with any archival spectrum or with the photometric Teff. An unchanged photosphere with new circumstellar Na I D / K I absorption points to an occulting disk. Changed line depths or temperature would point to an intrinsic or other cause. Pre-2014 archival photometry would show when the ingress began.

evidence.feature: Monotonic near-linear fade continued consistently across Gaia (0-1004 d), ZTF (1380-4060 d) and NEOWISE (-218 to 3415 d)
Identical fractional fade in ztf_g, ztf_r, ztf_i (~0.775) and BP/RP depth ratio 1.23 +/- 0.44 (z_grey 0.5)
W1/W2 fade by about the same fraction as the optical over the full baseline (W1 ~0.67 vs optical ~0.66); the neowise_change +0.15 is biased by fainter post-Gaia visits outside the window
Photospheric Ks-W1-W2 (W1-W2 ~ -0.1), no IR excess, W3/W4 upper limits only
Parallax SNR 19 at 850 pc gives M_G ~7 with BP-RP 1.3: main-sequence K dwarf, not a giant
35% decade-long fade far exceeds activity-cycle amplitudes, and a K dwarf cannot dim intrinsically by this much at constant colour
ruwe 0.99, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor: no resolved neighbour
Opaque-edge ingress at this rate implies a transverse speed ~1 m/s unless the edge is highly oblique; very fine-tuned
No recurrence, no eclipse-like shape, single slow trend (abbe 0.026, slope_z -49)

explanation: A quiet K dwarf (M_G ~7, no IR excess) fades almost linearly in flux by ~35% over ~11 yr, in Gaia, ZTF and NEOWISE alike. ZTF g, r and i drop by the same fraction (~0.775 between t~1400 and t~3670), BP/RP ratio is consistent with 1, and W1 fades about as much as the optical. Grey from 0.5 to 4.6 micron excludes small-grain dust and stellar cooling. Agreement between surveys excludes instrumental causes. The best known fit is a slow ingress of a large-grain or optically thick circumsecondary disk. That needs either a very gentle optical-depth gradient or an edge moving almost parallel to its own length. It is fine-tuned, so a large unexplained share remains.

discriminating_test: Check archival Gaia and NEOWISE light curves of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour for the same 2014-2017 decline. Then compare absolutely calibrated pre-2014 photometry (e.g. Pan-STARRS or SDSS) with today's ZTF level. This shows whether the fade is on this star, and whether it is a lasting grey drop or a brightening that came back down.

evidence.feature: BP/RP depth ratio 0.82+/-0.27 (z_grey -0.66, z_dust -3.24)
W1 visits at t<600 (1.08, 1.06, 1.03, 1.04, 1.02) brighter than later ~1.00, matching the G fade on an independent instrument
W1 change at least as large as G, where the Rayleigh-Jeans prediction for a star that cools is about a third of G
FOV1 and FOV2 agree at every paired epoch (e.g. t=1003-1004, 0.993-0.997 both)
ruwe 1.12, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp_excess 1.2
Smooth monotonic fade over ~1000+ d, then flat through ZTF 2018-2025 and NEOWISE to t~3600; no recurrence
Ingress lasting years needs a crossing speed far below orbital speed for any compact body
No infrared excess (Ks 13.8, W1 13.7, W2 13.7; W3/W4 upper limits)

explanation: This is a slow, steady fade, not a dip: about 3% in G from t~150 to t~1004 (abbe 0.08, slope_z -10.9), after which ZTF and NEOWISE stay flat. The fade is grey (BP/RP 0.82+/-0.27; interstellar-like dust ruled out at 3.2 sigma). NEOWISE W1 confirms it on its own: visits before t~600 are 3-5% brighter than later ones, at least as large as the change in G. That argues against a starspot or activity-driven temperature change, which would dim W1 less, and against a Gaia calibration drift. The two fields of view agree and there is no sign of a blend. The best natural reading is a slow partial occultation by large grains, such as a disk edge that has not yet moved off the star. No listed class fits well, so unexplained keeps a large share.

discriminating_test: Check ground-based archival photometry from the Gaia years (Catalina, ATLAS or Pan-STARRS, t=0-1000 d) for the same ~6% fade between t~180 and t~530 d. Compare with Gaia epoch photometry of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour taken on the same transits.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic G decline 1.055 to 0.99 over ~350 d then flat plateau; abbe 0.064
Early bright state seen in both fov 1 and fov 2 within the same transit pairs
BP and RP early epochs also ~4-7% above later median (noisy, ~1.5 sigma each)
Only 17 visits, G=17.8; early-mission epochs carry the whole signal
No scan_angle column; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 0.94, normal BP/RP excess
Plateau scatter close to errors in G and ZTF noise-dominated: star quiet on short timescales
NEOWISE W1/W2 unchanged; 1000 K shell prediction excluded at ~10 sigma; grey only ~1 sigma
Parallax SNR 3.8 at G=17.8 with bp_rp 1.29 implies K dwarf; W1-W2 ~ -0.2, no IR excess
Later ZTF g ~3% brighter after t~2830, smaller in r and i (bluer change)

explanation: This is not a dip. It is a smooth decline of about 6% between t~180 and t~530 d (Abbe 0.06, slope_z -6), after which the flux stays flat and quiet to the end of Gaia. Both fields of view show it, and BP and RP also sit a few per cent higher in the early epochs, so it may well be real. A faint K dwarf (parallax SNR 3.8, no IR excess, W1-W2 stellar) changing its long-term spot coverage over an activity cycle fits best. A slow calibration or scan-angle blend residual is a close alternative because there are only 17 visits. Eclipses are ruled out, and so is a hot dust shell (NEOWISE). ZTF is normalised per field, so it cannot test the Gaia level.

discriminating_test: Use archival pre-2014 multi-band photometry (CRTS, Pan-STARRS, SDSS or photographic plates) to find when the fade began and whether its onset was chromatic or had an ingress shape. Add one current spectrum to confirm that the spectral type is unchanged while the flux has dropped.

evidence.feature: Gaia G smooth monotonic fade, slope -3.61%/yr, slope_z -37.7, abbe 0.033; fov 1 and 2 pairs agree
Same fade continues in ZTF g, r, i from t~1400 to t~4060 at a matching rate in flux; NEOWISE also fades
Near-equal fractional fades in ztf_g (~0.29), ztf_r (~0.29), ztf_i (~0.26); BP/RP ratio 1.23 +/- 0.42
NEOWISE W1 ~1.2 to ~0.75 and W2 ~1.2 to ~0.75 over the span, as deep as the optical (grey to 4.6 micron; pred_dust_in_front and pred_star_temperature predict little W1 dimming)
Flux decline linear with no curvature over ~40% total loss; an opaque edge crossing a ~1.5 Rsun star in >11 yr implies mm/s speeds
parallax_snr 3.7, G-Ks ~1.4, normal BP/RP excess, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 0.95
Single long episode, no recurrence, star otherwise quiet (sigma_visit 0.0034)

explanation: The star fades smoothly and steadily, at a near-constant rate in flux, for about 11 years. Gaia G drops about 10% in 1000 d, ZTF g/r/i drop a further ~30% at the same rate, and NEOWISE W1/W2 fade by a similar ~35%. Three independent instruments agree, so it is not instrumental. The fade is grey from 0.5 to 4.6 micron: g, r and i are nearly equal, and W1 dims as much as G. That rules out interstellar-like dust, star cooling and spots. The only listed natural fit is a slowly deepening grey occultation by a large-grained circumsecondary disk. Even that needs an AU-scale smooth optical-depth gradient, because an opaque edge would have to move at mm/s. The fade shows no curvature or colour change, and the linear grey ramp looks unnatural.

discriminating_test: Get archival ATLAS or Pan-STARRS photometry spanning t~700-1400 (late 2016 to 2018). It would show whether the same chromatic fade appears in independent, better-resolved data and how and when it ended. A real occultation predicts a gradual or structured egress with the same colour; no fade there would point to a Gaia processing artefact or an injection.

evidence.feature: Step of 9% in G between t=733 and t=829 in both fields of view, flat at about 0.92 to the last visit (at least 175 d)
Fade lasting at least 175 d on a dwarf-sized star needs an occulter far larger than a star (t~2R/v)
BP/RP depth ratio 4.24+/-1.4 (z_grey 2.3, z_dust 1.8): chromatic, small-grain-like
Quiet before the drop and no added scatter after it, so no rotational modulation
ruwe 0.964, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.21 (normal for this colour)
ZTF 2018 onward is flat. Its faint outliers are about as many as its bright ones and follow the cadence, so there is no ongoing irregular dipping
NEOWISE excludes a 1000 K shell. The single in-fade W1 visit is uninformative
Box-flat bottom (scatter at noise level) and an onset the data do not resolve: looks like an injection or an artefact
Parallax detected at 3.9 sigma and G-Ks of about 1.8 match a stellar photosphere

explanation: A quiet K-type dwarf (bp_rp 1.08, sigma_visit 0.56%) dropped 9% in G sometime between t=733 and t=829. The drop shows in both fields of view and in G, BP and RP, and it stayed flat at about 0.92 until Gaia's last visit, at least 175 days later. The dimming is strongly chromatic (BP 16%, RP 3.8%, ratio 4.2+/-1.4, not grey), so it points to small dust grains. An occulter crossing in at least 175 days must be far larger than a star (t~2R/v), so the best fit is a dusty disk or cloud around a wide companion passing in front of the star. No blend shows (ruwe 0.96, no multi-peak fraction, normal BP/RP excess). The box-flat bottom and the sudden onset leave room for a processing artefact or an injection.

discriminating_test: Check whether Gaia G epochs of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour, observed in the same transits, show the same step between t=180 and t=302, or check independent 2014-2015 photometry (e.g. Pan-STARRS1 or Catalina) for a real 3% fade of this star across early 2015.

evidence.feature: G at ~1.03 for t=0-180 (both FoVs), then flat ~1.00 from t=302 to 930: a step, not a linear trend
Early high level not repeated at the same season in years 2 and 3 (t~456-555, 829-930), so not tied to recurring scan angles
ruwe 1.03, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.13 normal
ZTF g/r/i 2018-2024 flat (change after 2020 under 1%, slopes ~0), scatter equal to errors
BP/RP depth errors ~0.08, so the colour of a 3% change cannot be measured
bp_rp 1.06, G-Ks 1.9 at |b| 20-25 deg: K-type dwarf, no youth or IR-excess indicators
~1% visit-level wandering after the step (e.g. visits at t=462 and 1002 near 0.99)
No AllWISE photometry; NEOWISE W1/W2 too noisy (errors 6-25%) to test dust or temperature

explanation: The 'trend' is really a ~3% step. All six G epochs in the first 180 days sit near 1.03 in both fields of view. Every visit from t=302 to t=930 is flat near 1.00, with no slope, and ZTF in 2018-2024 is flat to within 1% in g, r and i. A one-off offset confined to the earliest mission epochs is most likely residual early-mission calibration or processing, not the star. Scan-angle blending is unlikely: the high level does not recur in the same season in later years, ruwe is 1.03 and there is no multi-peak signal. BP/RP are too noisy to give the colour. A real activity-level change in this K-type dwarf remains possible, weakly supported by ~1% visit-level wandering.

discriminating_test: Compare absolutely calibrated pre-Gaia photometry (e.g. Pan-STARRS1 2010-2014) with absolutely calibrated ZTF 2018+ magnitudes, and check Gaia epochs of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour. This tests whether the 7% drop is real and lasting on the star or a Gaia-only systematic.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic G decline to a plateau (abbe 0.089, slope_z -10.6), lasting about 450 d of ramp then at least 175 d flat
fov 1 and fov 2 transits agree throughout the fade; scatter within groups near t=457-459 is at the noise level
ruwe 0.984, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.2 (normal for bp_rp 0.88)
BP/RP depth ratio 0.872 +- 0.5 (z_grey -0.26, z_dust -1.66): grey-like but weak
ZTF g/r/i flat to about 1% for 7 years after Gaia, robust sigma close to the errors, no modulation
Quiet star with no rotational modulation in Gaia groups or ZTF, so a 7% activity-cycle change is unlikely
G-Ks about 1.5 is stellar for bp_rp 0.88; star at high galactic latitude with poorly constrained distance (probably old)

explanation: Gaia G falls smoothly by about 7%, from a level near 1.02 (t<360) to a plateau near 0.95 (t>830). The slope is significant (slope_z -10.6, abbe 0.09), both fields of view show it, and scatter within groups stays at the noise level. With ruwe 0.98, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0 and a normal BP/RP excess, blends and FoV/CCD artefacts are unlikely. The BP/RP depth ratio is 0.87+-0.5, so the colour could be grey but is barely constrained, and NEOWISE is too noisy to help. ZTF stays flat to about 1% over 2018-2025, with no rotational modulation. That argues against quasar variability and against a large spot cycle. The most probable cause is a slow, long-lasting occultation by circumstellar material, but no explanation stands out.

discriminating_test: Check independent multi-epoch photometry covering Gaia days ~300-600 (e.g. Pan-STARRS or CRTS), or differential Gaia epoch photometry of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour, to see whether the ~3% fade is on this star alone.

explanation: A faint (G=17.7), roughly solar-coloured source, probably a dwarf at a few kpc. It sits near 1.02 for about 360 d, falls about 3% during a 143 d data gap, then recovers slightly. The G fields of view agree, ruwe and the multi-peak and excess indicators show no neighbour, and BP and RP both fade (noisy). So the change looks real and broadband, but the colour ratio (1.27+/-0.92) cannot separate grey, dust or temperature. The likeliest causes are a slow brightness change of the star itself (activity) or a residual Gaia calibration offset specific to this source. A long grey occultation remains possible. ZTF stays flat from 2018 to 2023, which argues against AGN or ongoing irregular variability. No infrared data cover the event.

discriminating_test: Pull ATLAS c/o (or Pan-STARRS) photometry for mid-2016 to mid-2017, the dip window. An independent ~3.5% dip would confirm it is on the star, and its c/o depth ratio would separate grey disk material from interstellar-like dust or spots. A flat curve there would point to Gaia processing or calibration.

explanation: The pipeline calls this a trend, but the G light curve shows one dip: flat near 1.00 to t~555, slow ingress (t~680-830), a floor near 0.967 (t~830-911), then a faster recovery to 1.000 by t~1003. Both fields of view and several separate scan groups show it, so a FOV offset, a scan-angle blend or a one-epoch defect is unlikely. ZTF stays flat within ~1% for 7 years afterwards. The star looks like a quiet, old K dwarf at about 2 kpc. A ~3.5% dip lasting ~300 days needs an occulter far larger than the star (t~2R/v), which points to a disk or dust structure around a wide companion. Neither BP/RP nor WISE can test that.

explanation: A quiet G~16.7 star, probably a dwarf (parallax SNR 2.7, bp_rp 1.05, no IR excess, normal BP/RP excess, ruwe 1.03). The first three Gaia transit groups (t=0-152) sit about 3% high in G, BP and RP, and both fields of view agree. The level then drops sharply within 27 days and keeps fading by about 1%/yr until Gaia ends. ZTF later is flat. The drop is grey-to-mildly-red, which cannot be told apart given the BP error, and NEOWISE shows no change. It never recurs, so an eclipse or scan-angle blend is unlikely. The main options are a source-specific Gaia calibration or processing step in the early epochs, or a long occultation by a disk or dust that began sharply. Activity is unlikely because the star is otherwise very quiet. The packet cannot separate these.

discriminating_test: Check archival long-baseline photometry from before Gaia (e.g. CRTS/ASAS-SN/Pan-STARRS) for an earlier dimming of the same depth and colour. Finding one would fix a long period, pointing to a disk around a companion. Also take a few RVs to look for a long-period companion.

explanation: A quiet, roughly solar-type dwarf (M_G about 4, no IR excess) shows one ~10% dimming lasting 100-320 days: deep at t=329-405 in both fields of view and all three bands, half recovered at 428, normal by 552. The depths are self-consistent (G between BP and RP) and strongly chromatic (BP/RP ratio 2.05, grey excluded at 9 sigma, cooling of the star at ~5 sigma). NEOWISE W1 during the dip is unchanged, which rules out grey blocking and matches dust in front. Stellar eclipses cannot last this long. The most likely cause is small-grained dust, such as a circumsecondary disk or debris cloud, crossing the line of sight. No repeat appears in 7 years of ZTF, so any period is longer than ~10 years.

discriminating_test: Look up the scan angles of the first four Gaia transits and the epoch photometry of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour at the same times. If they show the same early excess, or it follows scan angle, it is instrumental. If neither is true, the star really was brighter in 2014; archival Pan-STARRS1 2010-2014 epochs could confirm that.

explanation: The 'trend' is not a steady fade. The first four Gaia G visits (t=0-179) sit 1.4-3.9% high and decline smoothly, and G stays flat near 1.00 from t=302 to 1003, so the late epochs are no fainter than the middle ones. The star is a main-sequence K dwarf (M_G about 7.4 at 1300 pc, no IR excess, ruwe 1.01). The likeliest cause is a slow change in its own magnetic activity or a residual early-mission Gaia calibration effect on a G=18 source. The colour test is uninformative (BP and RP too noisy). ZTF shows no continued change after Gaia (r change +0.05%, slopes near 0). W1 is also high before t=150, but that is weak evidence: faint-source NEOWISE visit means are noisy and W1 changes more than an occulter or a temperature change would allow.

explanation: The 'trend' is mostly a ~4% bright state in the first seven G epochs (t<180 d), followed by a flat level with a ~1% slow decline. ZTF afterwards shows no continued fade (+0.6%). Both fields of view agree, ruwe and IPD are clean, and BP/RP follow the change (depths ~0.10, noisy; ratio 1.01+/-0.47, so the colour tells us nothing). The parallax points to a distant, probably old K-type dwarf at high latitude, so a 5% activity-cycle change is possible but not typical. The lack of any IR excess argues against dust. The leading explanation is a calibration-epoch or processing offset, or a faint blend, affecting the early epochs. The alternative is genuine slow spot or activity variability. The packet is too thin to decide.

discriminating_test: Check pre-2014 archival photometry (Pan-STARRS1, SDSS, CRTS, APASS, photographic plates) to see when the fade began and whether the star was flat before. Also take one spectrum to look for a companion and for gas absorption from a disk that changes with time.

explanation: A G8-K0 dwarf (M_G about 5) at 1.7 kpc fades smoothly and almost linearly, losing about 4% of its flux per year for more than 11 years. The fade shows in Gaia G/BP/RP (BP/RP depth ratio 1.03), in ZTF g/r/i (each about 32% over 7 yr, so grey) and in NEOWISE W1/W2. Three instruments with different apertures agree, which rules out instrumental causes and blends. The fade is grey from g to 4.6 micron, which rules out stellar cooling and small dust and needs an opaque or large-grain occulter. The best known mechanism is the slow ingress of an optically thick circumsecondary disk whose optical depth changes gradually. But the very smooth, structureless, linear fade on an otherwise quiet star is not typical of real occultations, so the unexplained share stays large.

discriminating_test: Take a low-resolution spectrum plus a JHK epoch now, to confirm the photosphere is unchanged (same Teff, dwarf) and the fade is still grey into the near-IR, and look for new circumstellar gas absorption (e.g. Na D). Together with archival pre-2014 survey epochs, this pins the onset and shows whether the profile is an ingress.

explanation: A K dwarf (M_G about 6.9, bp_rp 1.42) has faded steadily by about 4%/yr since about 2014: Gaia G -10% over 1000 d, ZTF g/r/i about -30% over 7 yr, NEOWISE W1/W2 similar. The ZTF post-2020 changes are identical in g, r and i (-0.129/-0.128/-0.131), and W1 tracks the optical, so the fade is grey from 0.5 to 4.6 micron. That rules out small dust, cooling and spots, and there is no IR brightening from re-radiation. Three independent instruments agree, which excludes artefacts. Best fit: a slow ingress into an optically thick or large-grained disk on our sightline. A sharp edge would have to move at about 1 m/s, so a smooth optical-depth gradient over AU scales is needed. That is unusual, so unexplained keeps substantial weight.

discriminating_test: Get Gaia DR4 epoch photometry (to 2020) with scan angles, and compare against field stars of similar magnitude. If the fade persists or slowly recovers independent of scan angle and is not shared, the cause is stellar (activity cycle); if it tracks scan angle or calibration intervals, it is instrumental. Also check whether field stars show the same pre-2016 NEOWISE W1 offset.

explanation: A near-solar dwarf (M_G about 5, BP-RP 0.9) fades smoothly by about 0.6-1% in G, BP and RP over roughly 2 years (slope_z -5.4, abbe 0.23). Both fields of view agree, and the star is quiet from visit to visit (0.16%). The most likely cause is slow stellar brightness change, such as a magnetic activity cycle shifting spot and facula coverage. The colour ratio (1.42 +/- 0.84) fits a temperature change as well as grey blocking. A residual Gaia calibration or processing drift specific to this source is the main alternative. A hot dust shell is excluded by W1. Eclipses are disfavoured: the fade has no egress and ruwe is 1.0. Against all of these, W1 sits about 3.7% higher before the fade, which no dust or temperature model predicts and may be a NEOWISE systematic.

A ~3% drop in ATLAS confirms the change is in the star; a matching step in the neighbours makes it a calibration artefact.

The order is clean (no early visit is fainter than any later one), which argues against a neighbour entering the window at random scan angles. BP is too noisy for a colour test. The RP depth (0.030+-0.018) matches G. NEOWISE is too noisy, and ZTF (2018 on, flat) is normalised, so it cannot be tied to Gaia's level. This looks like a G/K dwarf with no IR excess and W1-W2 about -0.2, so not an AGN. Best guess: a real long-term change in spot or facula coverage, with a source-specific Gaia calibration step close behind. The packet excludes neither.

They appear in Gaia G/BP/RP in both fields of view, in ZTF g/r/i and in NEOWISE W1. The depth is grey and stays the same over about 13 cycles. The star is a quiet G8-K0 dwarf (M_G about 5) with no IR excess and normal RUWE. Agreement across surveys rules out instrumental causes. An eclipse obeys t~2R/v: at P=284 d, v is about 32 km/s, so an 80 d dip needs an occulter about 1.5 AU long, larger than the 0.85 AU orbit. That is about 100 times too long for a stellar or planetary transit and too large for any bound circumsecondary disk. Only an unlikely KH 15D-like screen remains, so no listed class fits well.

A shared or scan-angle-correlated ~4% early offset would make this instrumental. If there is none, a stellar activity change (spots or chromosphere) remains the best explanation.

This is a level change, not a dip that recovers. The band ordering BP (5.8%) > G (4.0%) > RP (0.8%) and an unchanged W1 at t=330, while G was still ~3% high, rule out grey blocking. They favour a chromatic change in the star itself, most likely a shift in spot or activity level. Against that, RP falls about 2 sigma short of what a temperature change predicts, so a G-only instrumental step or an unphysical signal cannot be excluded. Dust occultation, eclipses and YSO behaviour fit poorly.

discriminating_test: Inspect the individual NEOWISE W1/W2 exposures and images from the in-dip visit (t about 330) for a moving object, ghost or latent artefact, and check whether the excess sits on the star in every exposure; if real and stable, the hot-dust interpretation firms up greatly.

Single in-dip NEOWISE visit: W1 +0.545, W2 +1.27, both above the 1000 K shell prediction (0.405, 0.864) and near its colour; adjacent visits normal

explanation: A transient circumstellar dust cloud, most likely debris, around a field K7-M0 dwarf (M_G about 7.6, photospheric Ks/W1/W2, no AllWISE excess). The G fade deepens from 4% to 10% over 55 d on three visits and agrees between both fields of view. RP fades less than G, which fits small grains; BP is too noisy to use. The one NEOWISE visit inside the dip shows W1 +54% and W2 +127%, the colour of dust at about 900-1000 K re-emitting about 9-10% of the star's light. That fits the energy budget for dust near 0.02 AU. Both IR visits on either side are normal and ZTF stays quiet for years, so this looks like a one-off dust event, not an eclipse or a YSO disk.

discriminating_test: Compare Gaia G epoch photometry for nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour on the same transits, and Gaia DR4 epochs overlapping ZTF 2018-2020. If the early-high/late-low pattern is shared, or G keeps fading while ZTF stays flat, it is instrumental. If G follows ZTF g, it is real low-level variability; a low-resolution spectrum would then separate a star from a quasar.

explanation: A weak (slope_z -3.75, 18 visits) ~3% G decline in a faint G=18.8 source. Most of the trend comes from two high visits at the very start of the mission and two low visits at the end (t=927, 1004), and the middle is roughly flat, so it looks more like offsets between calibration epochs or residual faint-end drift than a steady fade. Both fields of view show it. BP/RP are far too noisy to give a colour (ratio undefined), and there is no IR. ZTF from 2018-2024 is flat to about 2% in r and i, so the fade does not continue. Low-level stellar activity, or a weakly variable quasar (smooth wander, slightly larger in ZTF g), are the main astrophysical options.

discriminating_test: Compare the star's absolute calibrated magnitudes, not median-normalised ones, from Pan-STARRS1 (2010-2014), Gaia and calibrated ZTF, transformed to one band. This tests whether the fade is a real, lasting and chromatic change of the star. Check at the same time whether any catalogued neighbour within 3 arcsec varies.

evidence.feature: G trend -2.05%/yr, slope_z -7.83, Abbe 0.151; the paired FoV 1/FoV 2 transits agree at every epoch
sigma_visit 0.0054 is about the photometric noise, so there is little short-term or rotational variability despite a 5% long-term change
BP depth 0.195+/-0.067 against RP 0.028+/-0.038; ratio 6.96+/-9.72 (z_grey 0.61, z_dust 0.54), uninformative
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.23 is normal for bp_rp 1.16; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0; ruwe 0.986
BP and RP scatter well above their errors (robust sigma 0.10 against 0.036, and 0.062 against 0.024); the first four visit groups are high in all bands
ZTF 2018-2024 has no continuing 2%/yr fade (r change +0.2%, slopes about 0), though offsets of each field are normalised away
parallax_snr 2.8 at G=18 implies a dwarf at a few kpc
no AllWISE photometry, and the NEOWISE W1 slope -0.055+/-0.143 cannot test dust re-emission or dimming

explanation: Most probable: the K-type dwarf really faded by about 5%, probably through a change in its magnetic activity or spot coverage, though instrumental and unexplained causes are almost as likely. G falls smoothly from about 1.035 to 0.98 over 1000 d (slope_z -7.8, Abbe 0.15), the same in both fields of view, so it is not an offset between them. The BP/RP excess factor, IPD and RUWE show no neighbour. BP fades more than RP, as cooling or reddening would cause, but the colour ratio (7 +/- 10) cannot tell grey, dust and temperature apart. Against a spot cycle, the star is otherwise quiet: its visit-to-visit scatter is about the noise level. ZTF shows no continued fade in 2018-2024, but normalising each field hides the absolute level. There is no mid-IR photometry to test for dust.

discriminating_test: Check the transit-level data for the two dip transits (t=302.5 and 332.7): per-CCD G fluxes, across-scan window position or truncation, and scan angle, compared with other transits at similar scan angles. A truncated or edge window, or a neighbour in that direction, makes the dip instrumental. A uniform deficit on all 9 CCDs in a normal window makes it real.

evidence.feature: Dip defined by only two G epochs (302.46, 332.70), each a single fov-2 transit with no paired 106.5-min transit, in consecutive visits; other single fov-2 transits (t=0, 679) are normal
BP brightens at both dip epochs (1.22, 1.30); depth_bp -0.179+/-0.098, ratio_bp_over_rp -2.54+/-2.02; BP and RP scatter well above their errors
RP 0.837 at 332.7 tracks G 0.80, but RP 1.05 at 302.5 does not track G 0.88; RP shows similar ~15% outliers without G dips (913.1, 1002.4)

Normal G at 179.1 and 357.7 on either side; depth grows from 12% to 20% over 30 d; implied crossing speed of only ~0.05-0.3 km/s for a 0.6 Rsun star, so the occulter would have to be large and extended
NEOWISE visit at 330.8: W1 -6.8+/-6.1%, W2 -12.8+/-12.5%, close to the grey prediction (-10.9%); the 1000 K shell (+62%/+132%) is excluded
bp_rp 1.89, M_G ~8.4 at 930 pc: an early M dwarf; Ks-W1 0.2 and W1-W2 0.1 show no IR excess
Otherwise quiet: G robust sigma 0.97% close to the errors, abbe 0.68, slope_z 0.87; ZTF g/r/i flat from 2018 with no level change after 2020
ZTF r has 9 faint singletons at 13-21% out of 1316 epochs, but its outlier tails are symmetric (27 above, 21 below 3 sigma) and ZTF i has none
ruwe 1.02, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor 1.32: no close resolved neighbour or astrometric companion

explanation: The most likely cause is a Gaia transit-level artefact. The 'episode' rests on just two G transits, t=302.5 (0.88) and t=332.7 (0.80). Each is a lone fov-2 transit whose paired transit is missing, and they come from consecutive visits that probably share a scan geometry, which fits window-edge flux loss or neighbour contamination. BP is brighter at both epochs, not fainter (ratio -2.5+/-2.0), and RP dims only at the second, so the bands do not agree the way an occulter needs them to. A real alternative is still possible: an early M dwarf with no IR excess, roughly grey-dimmed for 30-178 d by a companion's disk or dust. RP at 332.7 and a slightly faint NEOWISE visit at 330.8 weakly support that. The star is otherwise quiet.
